title: The 8 Levels of Rent
house: A bustling neon-lit metropolis called Produce City, where concrete skyscrapers tower over crowded subway stations, smoky late-night diners, and tight-knit apartment buildings.

levels.name: Mia, 21, Intern
levels.story: The 8 levels of rent. Level 1. Level 1: $450 a month rent for a tiny converted closet, and my glowing forehead badge screams my total shame to the entire subway car. I am Mia, a 21-year-old blueberry person with blue skin and a nervous twitch, working three unpaid internships just to survive in this brutal city. Yesterday, my best friend invited me to their sleek downtown loft to compare our monthly rent bills over expensive takeout. You cannot afford the air in this room. My rent is higher than your entire yearly savings account. Tears welled up behind my blue berry skin, but I refused to let them see me break. Then, my phone buzzed in my pocket with an anonymous text message containing a photo of a bank transfer that changed everything. What was hidden inside the ripped envelope left by the landlord? You'll see that in Level 2.

levels.name: Leo, 24, Barista
levels.story: The 8 levels of rent. Level 2. Level 2: $850 a month rent for a basement studio, and my forehead badge makes me the joke of the whole cafe. I am Leo, a bright yellow lemon person with a sour twist in my smile, slinging espresso shots for ungrateful tech bros. Last night, our group of friends gathered at the neon noodle bar to compare rent checks, and my badge glowed pathetically next to the others. Working eighty hours a week just to sleep in a damp basement is a choice. My citrus skin tightened in absolute fury as the entire room turned to stare at me. I gripped my damp apron strings until my knuckles turned white. Then, my phone lit up with a notification that proved someone had secretly paid my entire past-due balance. Who transferred the exact amount of last month's unpaid rent to her account? You'll see that in Level 3.

levels.name: Sam, 28, Graphic Designer
levels.story: The 8 levels of rent. Level 3. Level 3: $1,400 a month rent for a shared apartment, and my badge makes me feel invisible next to my roommate's lavish lifestyle. I am Sam, an orange person with bright citrus segments for skin, juggling freelance design gigs while surviving on instant coffee. Tonight, our tight-knit friend group met in the cluttered kitchen to compare monthly housing costs over cheap wine. You call this a home? It is just a glorified storage unit with a bed. My orange skin burned with humiliation as the others nodded in fake sympathy. I swallowed the lump in my throat, refusing to let them see my tears. Then, the front door buzzer rang, and the delivery person handed me a heavy manila envelope with a red wax seal. What was written in the confidential letter left on the kitchen table? You'll see that in Level 4.

levels.name: Chloe, 26, Accountant
levels.story: The 8 levels of rent. Level 4. Level 4: $2,200 a month rent for a one-bedroom apartment, and my badge puts me right in the exhausting middle class trap. I am Chloe, a crisp broccoli person with curly green florets for hair, crunching numbers all day at a corporate firm. Today during lunch break at the rooftop park, our friend circle gathered to compare our monthly housing overhead. Paying two grand just to hear your neighbors snoring through the drywall is pathetic. My green floret hair bristled with anger as I gripped my salad container until the plastic cracked. I held my breath, refusing to give him the satisfaction of seeing me cry. Then, my phone buzzed with an urgent email alert from the city housing authority. Who sent the anonymous tip to the building inspector about the illegal loft modification? You'll see that in Level 5.

levels.name: Max, 31, Software Engineer
levels.story: The 8 levels of rent. Level 5. Level 5: $3,400 a month rent for a modern downtown high-rise, and my forehead badge makes me think I've finally made it. I am Max, a dragonfruit person with magenta skin and spiky green-tipped scales, writing code for a tech startup. Last Friday at the rooftop lounge, our friend group met to compare our monthly housing expenses over craft cocktails. If you cannot even pay three thousand for rent, maybe you should move back to the suburbs. Her blue skin flushed with deep embarrassment as the surrounding tables turned to watch. I smiled, feeling untouchable in my success. Then, the lounge manager rushed over with an urgent notice regarding a building-wide lease audit. What secret document did the property manager accidentally leave inside the unlocked safe? You'll see that in Level 6.

levels.name: Elena, 35, Architect
levels.story: The 8 levels of rent. Level 6. Level 6: $5,200 a month rent for a designer penthouse, and my forehead badge makes everyone treat me like royalty. I am Elena, a sleek coconut person with a polished hard brown shell and silver hoop earrings, designing mega-structures across Produce City. Tonight at our elite rooftop gathering, the wealthiest friends met to compare our luxury housing costs. Anyone can rent a fancy penthouse when they inherit their parents architectural firm. My brown coconut shell grew cold with fury as I stared him down without blinking. I refused to let his petty jealousy ruin my hard-earned triumph. Then, my tablet lit up with a breaking news alert about a massive corporate real estate takeover. Who was the mysterious investor buying up every single apartment building in the district? You'll see that in Level 7.

levels.name: Zoe, 29, Urban Mystic
levels.story: The 8 levels of rent. Level 8. Level 8: Priceless rent for a home that exists outside of money, and my forehead badge finally exposes the terrifying truth behind Produce City. I am Zoe, a glowing starfruit person with translucent golden skin shaped like five-point stars and amethyst eyes, watching the entire city from the highest spire. Tonight, all eight levels of friends, enemies, and landlords gathered in the central plaza for the final rent reckoning. You do not even pay rent because you own nothing at all in this city. My golden starfruit skin pulsed with brilliant light as I smiled down at every single person in the plaza. The numbers on our foreheads flickered simultaneously, shifting from currency to something far more powerful. What secret did the numbers on everyone's forehead actually mean all along? Which topic about money or status should we explore in our brand new series next?
